addressed_problems.content: Scaling NF-Layers to process the weights of very large networks remains an open challenge. The current NF-Layer design produces activation sizes that grow with the network's depth and channel dimensions, which can become a bottleneck for both memory and computation when applied to large-scale models. Future work is needed to develop strategies for reducing these activation sizes and improving the overall parameter and compute efficiency of permutation equivariant neural functionals, thereby enabling their application to weight spaces of significantly larger architectures.

Extending the NF-Layer framework to handle the weight spaces of more complex architectures beyond basic feedforward and convolutional networks is an open direction. Specifically, the framework currently does not address the unique structures of ResNet-style architectures (e.g., skip connections and normalization layers) or Transformer blocks (e.g., attention parameter tensors, layer normalization, and residual connections). Developing equivariant parameter-sharing schemes for these components, including how to treat flattened spatial layouts when convolutional outputs are fed into fully connected layers, would allow neural functionals to process weights from a much broader class of modern deep learning models.

A further open problem is defining the appropriate permutation action and equivariant parameter-sharing for neural network architectures with mixed or nonstandard wiring patterns. For instance, when spatial dimensions from a convolutional layer are flattened into a fully connected layer, the natural permutation symmetries may not be fully captured by existing NF-Layer definitions. Determining practical strategies to handle such cases—where different layer types interact in ways that break simple row/column permutation rules—is necessary to generalize permutation equivariant neural functionals to arbitrary network topologies.

An empirical open question concerns the conditions under which IO-encoding (positional embeddings added to input and output neurons) suffices to break input/output symmetry when using the parameter-efficient NP NF-Layer, versus when the fuller HNP parameter sharing is necessary. In particular, for tasks with very large input or output dimensions (n0 or nL), the performance gap between the two approaches may widen, and the trade-off between parameter efficiency and expressive power is not yet well understood. Systematic investigation of this trade-off across different tasks and dimensionalities would inform practical design choices for constructing permutation equivariant neural functionals.

Deep learning applications increasingly require functions that take other networks' parameters (weights, biases, gradients, sparsity masks) as input — for example, learned optimizers, inference over implicit neural representations (INRs), corrective model editing, policy evaluation, and identifying sparse initializations ("winning tickets"). A core scientific obstacle in designing such neural functionals is that feedforward network weight spaces possess nontrivial permutation symmetries: permuting the neurons of a hidden layer (and thus permuting the corresponding rows and columns of adjacent weight matrices and the bias entries) leaves network input-output behavior unchanged. Prior approaches either (a) hand-design ad hoc, task-specific statistics of weights (e.g., moments, spectral summaries) that may miss complex weight-space correlations, or (b) train generic neural networks on flattened weight vectors possibly augmented by random permutation data-augmentation to encourage permutation robustness. These prior strategies suffer from concrete limitations: hand-designed features can omit informative higher-order structure and provide limited predictive power; standard feedforward predictors do not enforce permutation equivariance and therefore must learn invariance from data (data-inefficient and brittle); naive equivariance via data augmentation is costly and may fail to generalize across permutations; and a principled architecture that processes raw weight-space features while respecting neuron permutation symmetry is missing. Practically, these gaps prevent reliable, data-efficient, and scalable neural functionals that (i) capture correlations across weights and layers induced by permutation symmetry, (ii) generalize across re-orderings of neurons, and (iii) scale parameter- and compute-wise to realistic architectures (e.g., when input or output dimensions are large as in classification). This work is motivated by the need for a unifying, symmetry-aware architectural framework that (1) mathematically characterizes linear maps on weight space that respect neuron permutation symmetries, (2) yields practical, parameter-efficient layer implementations for both strong and weaker symmetry assumptions, and (3) can be composed into nonlinear neural functionals that are empirically effective on diverse weight-space tasks.

nodes.content: In weight-space processing, designers need primitive linear transformations that (i) exactly satisfy the neuron-permutation symmetry induced by treating all neurons (including inputs and outputs) as exchangeable, and (ii) are expressive enough to represent any linear map that respects this symmetry so that composing these primitives with pointwise nonlinearities suffices to build general equivariant neural functionals. Prior practice lacked a compact, explicit algebraic description of such linear primitives: the generic linear map on flattened weight vectors has $\dim(\mathcal{U})^2$ parameters and does not enforce equivariance, requiring expensive learning to approximate symmetry; data augmentation does not guarantee exact equivariance and is sample-inefficient. Without a principled characterization one cannot both enforce symmetry exactly and retain completeness (ability to represent all linear equivariant maps), which impedes constructing sound, composable, and efficient equivariant NFNs.

Many practical weight-space tasks (e.g., classifying INRs, editing INRs, predicting generalization) involve networks whose inputs and outputs are inherently ordered (so input/output neurons should not be permuted), making the full $\mathcal{S}$ assumption too strong. Designers therefore require linear NF-Layers that are equivariant only to hidden-layer permutations ($\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$) and which correctly treat input/output dimensions as ordered. Simply applying the NP-layer $H$ would incorrectly tie parameters across input/output indices or require breaking symmetry ad hoc; conversely, naively keeping a fully unconstrained linear map leads to intractable parameter counts and loss of equivariance. A concrete, index-wise parameter-sharing prescription for the HNP case is necessary to both enforce the physically-correct symmetry and yield a usable layer; prior work lacked a compact HNP parameter-sharing specification that accounts for boundary layers (input/output) and yields practical parameter counts.

Many downstream tasks (e.g., scalar prediction of test accuracy, classification heads) require outputs invariant to neuron permutations. Without a modular invariant readout that deterministically collapses equivariant weight-space features to invariant summaries, one either must learn invariance from data (inefficient) or risk producing symmetry-violating outputs. An explicit invariant NF-Layer that is compatible with the equivariant NF-Layers resolves how to convert equivariant feature maps into invariant vectors in a principled, parameter-efficient way.

Many practical weight-space inputs are convolutional (e.g., image classifiers), where neurons correspond to output channels and filters possess spatial dimensions that are not permuted. A naive NF-Layer formulation for fully connected weights does not immediately account for non-permuted spatial filter dimensions. Without an explicit extension, equivariant NF-Layers would be restricted to fully connected inputs or require special-case engineering per CNN architecture. Folding spatial filter dimensions into the channel axis provides a principled way to reuse the NF-Layer design for convolutional weight spaces while preserving the correct permutation action on channel indices.

The NP-equivariant layer $H$ is significantly more parameter-efficient than the HNP layer $\tilde{H}$, but strictly imposing full neuron permutation symmetry (including inputs and outputs) is often incorrect for tasks where inputs and outputs are ordered (e.g., image pixel coordinates, classification labels). Designers therefore face a dilemma: use $\tilde{H}$ (correct but often prohibitively parameter-heavy when $n_0$ or $n_L$ are large) or use $H$ (efficient but enforces incorrect IO symmetry). A mechanism is needed to retain $H$'s parameter efficiency while selectively breaking input/output symmetry. IO-encoding provides such a mechanism by supplying positional cues that break unwanted symmetries, enabling the efficient NP-layer to model IO-asymmetric behavior.

Designers need quantitative guidance about how symmetry assumptions affect model size and scalability: a fully unconstrained linear map on flattened weight vectors is infeasible for large weight spaces; imposing full neuron permutation symmetry dramatically reduces parameter count, but may over-tie parameters when input/output dimensions are ordered; imposing only hidden-layer permutation symmetry is more flexible but can reintroduce dependence on $n_0$ and $n_L$ that may be large. Concrete asymptotic parameter counts are required to make informed choices about which equivariance assumption is practical for a given application.

Predicting test accuracy from trained network weights is a data-driven approach to studying generalization, but prior methods relied either on hand-crafted statistics of weights (STATNN) that may miss richer weight-space structure, or on generic predictors that do not encode permutation symmetries, forcing the model to learn invariance from data. This results in suboptimal predictive performance and sample inefficiency. A neural functional that exactly respects the correct HNP symmetry and can process the full weight tensors is expected to extract more informative features and thus improve correlation with held-out test accuracy.

INRs encode images or 3D shapes as network weights; extracting semantic information (e.g., class labels) from INR weights requires architectures that can discover relationships across a network's parameters while respecting neuron permutation symmetries. Prior non-equivariant approaches (standard MLPs or inr2vec) either ignore symmetry or assume shared initializations, leading to poor generalization, difficulty fitting training data under permutation augmentation, and inability to exploit cross-weight correlations. Equivariant NFNs provide a symmetry-aware architecture that can process raw INR weights and produce invariant summaries for classification, addressing the representational and generalization deficits of prior methods.

Finding winning-ticket sparsity masks without training (i.e., from initialization alone) is challenging: IMP finds masks by pruning trained models, which is computationally expensive and not predictive at initialization. Prior attempts struggle to generalize mask prediction across initializations. A symmetry-aware generative model that conditions on the initialization and outputs sparsity masks could enable predicting high-quality masks cheaply; to be effective it must process initialization weight tensors while respecting neuron permutation symmetries. The NFN-based cVAE addresses this by using equivariant encoder/decoder NF-Layers to learn a conditional distribution over masks.

Editing the semantic content of an INR (e.g., dilating shapes, changing contrast) by directly manipulating its weights requires a function that understands how weight changes map to coordinated pixel-level changes; naive pointwise weight perturbations or MLP predictors that ignore permutation structure fail to produce coherent global edits. A neural functional that can process the entire weight structure and produce coordinated, permutation-consistent edits is necessary to produce image-space edits that match classical image-processing operations. Equivariant NFNs address this by using NF-Layers to capture cross-weight interactions that correspond to geometric and intensity transformations in the decoded image.

It is unclear which weight-space tasks require modeling cross-weight interactions versus those that can be solved by per-parameter scoring. For identifying winning tickets, simple heuristics like magnitude-based pruning can be effective; whether learned predictors need to model interactions affects model complexity. Demonstrating that a pointwise NFN variant suffices for mask prediction but not for editing clarifies which tasks demand full NF-Layer expressivity and which can use lighter-weight architectures.

To translate the theoretical NF-Layer constructions into usable architectures and to enable reproducibility and follow-up work, practitioners require concrete implementations and reference code. Without pseudocode and a public repository, applying the equivariant NF-Layers to real datasets and architectures would be hindered by engineering gaps.

A linear neuron-permutation-equivariant neural functional layer $H$ mapping $\mathcal{U}^{c_i} \to \mathcal{U}^{c_o}$ (where $\mathcal{U}^{c}$ denotes the direct sum of $c$ copies of weight space $\mathcal{U}$ consisting of weights $\{W^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i\times n_{i-1}\times c}\}_{i=1}^L$ and biases $\{v^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i\times c}\}_{i=1}^L$) is given by the per-entry formula (shown for single channel, $c_i=c_o=1$):
      $$
      H(W)_{j k}^{(i)} = \left(\sum_{s=1}^{L} a^{i,s} W_{\star,\star}^{(s)}\right) + b^{i,i} W_{\star,k}^{(i)} + b^{i,i-1} W_{k,\star}^{(i-1)} + c^{i,i} W_{j,\star}^{(i)} + c^{i,i+1} W_{\star,j}^{(i+1)} + d^{i} W_{j k}^{(i)},
      $$
      where $W_{\star,\star}^{(s)}$ sums over both row and column indices of $W^{(s)}$, $W_{\star,k}^{(i)}$ sums over rows, $W_{j,\star}^{(i)}$ sums over columns, and $W_{jk}^{(i)}$ is the element at position $(j,k)$ of layer $i$. In the multi-channel case, each $W_{jk}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{c_i}$ and each scalar parameter becomes a $c_o\times c_i$ matrix. The layer $H$ is equivariant to the neuron permutation group $\mathcal{S}=\prod_{i=0}^L S_{n_i}$ acting on weight-space features by permuting rows of $W^{(i)}$ by $\sigma_i$ and columns by $\sigma_{i-1}\colon [\sigma W]_{jk}^{(i)} = W_{\sigma_i^{-1}(j),\sigma_{i-1}^{-1}(k)}^{(i)}$ and $[\sigma v]_{j}^{(i)} = v_{\sigma_i^{-1}(j)}^{(i)}$. Moreover, every linear $\mathcal{S}$-equivariant map $T:\mathcal{U}^{c_i}\to\mathcal{U}^{c_o}$ is representable in this form for some choice of parameter matrices $a^{i,s},b^{i,\cdot},c^{i,\cdot},d^i$ (i.e., $H$ completely characterizes linear $\mathcal{S}$-equivariant maps).

metadata.narrative: The derivation of the NP-equivariant NF-Layer is supported by a formal proof of completeness (H1), which establishes that the layer can represent any linear S-equivariant map. No load-bearing uncertainties were identified; the derivation is mathematically sound. The layer therefore provides a principled building block for equivariant neural functionals.

nodes.title: NP-equivariant linear NF-Layer and its completeness for linear S-equivariant maps

nodes.content: For an $L$-layer feedforward network with layer sizes $n_0,\dots,n_L$, let $\mathcal{U}$ denote its weight space (weights $W^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i\times n_{i-1}}$ and biases $v^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i}$), and $\mathcal{U}^c$ the direct sum of $c$ copies. For the hidden neuron permutation group $\tilde{\mathcal{S}} = \prod_{i=1}^{L-1} S_{n_i}$, which permutes only hidden-layer neurons, the $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$-equivariant linear NF-Layer $\tilde{H}:\mathcal{U}^{c_i}\to\mathcal{U}^{c_o}$ is derived by computing equivariant parameter-sharing patterns for the parameter tensor $\theta$ of the flattened linear map. The parameter sharing partitions $\theta$ into orbits under the action of $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$, resulting in constraints that tie parameters across weight and bias indices. These constraints differ based on the layer indices $(i,s)$ and whether the layers are input ($i=1$), output ($i=L$), or hidden ($1<i<L$), introducing additional parameters that depend on the input dimension $n_0$ and output dimension $n_L$. After applying this sharing, $\tilde{H}$ has $O(c_i c_o (L + n_0 + n_L)^2)$ free parameter blocks.

metadata.narrative: The HNP parameter sharing tables provide a concrete specification (H2), but the completeness of the derivation is not as rigorously established as for the NP case (P1). The orbit analysis is plausible but not proven step-by-step, leaving a residual risk that the characterization is incomplete. However, the practical utility of the layer may not depend on full completeness, and H2 ensures that a usable layer exists. The conclusion's theoretical claim of "full" HNP layer is partially exposed by P1.

nodes.title: HNP-equivariant NF-Layer parameter sharing and complexity

nodes.content: Two invariant NF-Layers map weight-space features to permutation-invariant vectors by summing or averaging over axes with permutation symmetry. Under the full neuron-permutation group $\mathcal{S}=\prod_{i=0}^L S_{n_i}$, the $\mathcal{S}$-invariant layer $P:\mathcal{U}\to\mathbb{R}^{2L}$ is given by $P(U) = (W_{\star,\star}^{(1)},\ldots,W_{\star,\star}^{(L)}, v_{\star}^{(1)},\ldots,v_{\star}^{(L)})$, where $W_{\star,\star}^{(i)}$ denotes summation over both row and column indices of $W^{(i)}$ and $v_{\star}^{(i)}$ denotes summation over entries of $v^{(i)}$. Under the hidden neuron permutation group $\tilde{\mathcal{S}} = \prod_{i=1}^{L-1} S_{n_i}$, the $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$-invariant layer $\tilde{P}:\mathcal{U}\to\mathbb{R}^{2L+n_0+2n_L}$ is defined by $\tilde{P}(U) = (P(U), W_{\star,:}^{(1)}, W_{:,\star}^{(L)}, v^{(L)})$, where $W_{\star,:}^{(1)}$ sums over rows only (preserving the column index) and $W_{:,\star}^{(L)}$ sums over columns only (preserving the row index). Composing these invariant layers atop stacks of equivariant NF-Layers produces invariant neural functionals.

metadata.narrative: The invariant NF-Layers are defined by simple summation over permutable axes, a standard and uncontroversial construction. No load-bearing uncertainties were identified, and no element of the derivation rises above the field's default to warrant a highlight.

nodes.title: Invariant NF-Layers for NP and HNP symmetries producing permutation-invariant summaries

nodes.content: The NP-equivariant NF-Layer $H$ (defined for feedforward weight spaces where each layer $i$ has $n_i$ neurons) extends to convolutional weight spaces by treating channel and spatial filter dimensions as additional non-permuted channels. For a 1D CNN with filters $W^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_i \times n_{i-1} \times w}$ (where $n_i$ is the number of output channels, $n_{i-1}$ is the number of input channels, and $w$ is the filter width), define $W_{jk}^{(i)} := W_{j,k,:}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^w$ and fold the filter width into the channel dimension, so that $H$ acts on $W^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_i \times n_{i-1} \times (c w)}$ when processing $c$-channel features. This construction generalizes to 2D convolutions by similarly combining spatial dimensions into channels, allowing the same NF-Layer machinery to process CNN weight-space inputs.

metadata.narrative: The extension to convolutional weight spaces by folding spatial dimensions into the channel dimension is a natural and mechanically straightforward application of the multi-channel NF-Layer formulation. No load-bearing uncertainties were identified.

nodes.title: Extension of NF-Layers to convolutional weight spaces

nodes.content: To reconcile the parameter efficiency of the NP-equivariant layer $H$ (which assumes full neuron permutation symmetry $\mathcal{S} = \prod_{i=0}^L S_{n_i}$) with tasks requiring that input and output neurons be treated asymmetrically, IO-encoding adds learned or fixed sinusoidal positional embeddings to the columns of the first weight $W^{(1)}$, the rows of the last weight $W^{(L)}$, and the last bias $v^{(L)}$. These embeddings break permutations on input and output neurons while retaining the NP parameter sharing, enabling $H$ to model functions that are not symmetric with respect to input/output neurons. Empirically, IO-encoding makes $H$ competitive with or superior to the HNP-equivariant layer $\tilde{H}$ (which explicitly accounts for asymmetry) while using far fewer parameters when input and output dimensions are large.

metadata.narrative: The IO-encoding mechanism is empirically validated on INR classification and editing tasks, but no formal guarantee of sufficiency is provided. No load-bearing weaknesses were identified because the conclusion is bounded to the demonstrated experimental settings; however, the lack of a highlight indicates that the evidence is not unusually strong beyond standard empirical validation.

nodes.title: IO-encoding: positional encoding to break input/output symmetry for NP layers

nodes.content: For an $L$-layer feedforward network with input dimension $n_0$, output dimension $n_L$, and $c_i$, $c_o$ input and output channels, the number of free parameter blocks after equivariant parameter sharing scales as follows: the NP-equivariant layer $H$ has $O(c_i c_o L^2)$ free parameter blocks; the HNP-equivariant layer $\tilde{H}$ has $O(c_i c_o (L + n_0 + n_L)^2)$ free parameter blocks; and an unconstrained linear map would have $c_i c_o \dim(\mathcal{U})^2$ parameters, where $\dim(\mathcal{U})$ is the total dimensionality of the weight space ($\mathcal{U}$ includes all weights and biases). These asymptotic counts quantify the parameter-efficiency tradeoff between symmetry assumptions.

metadata.narrative: The parameter-count scaling is a direct consequence of the parameter-sharing tables for NP and HNP. The asymptotic bounds are straightforward to derive from the tables and are not in dispute.

nodes.title: Parameter-count scaling for NF-Layers under different symmetry assumptions

nodes.content: On the Small CNN Zoo benchmark subsets CIFAR-10-GS and SVHN-GS, an invariant neural functional network (NFN) built from the HNP-equivariant NF-Layer (denoted $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$) attains higher rank-correlation with test accuracy (Kendall's $\tau$) than both the NP variant ($\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$) and the prior STATNN baseline (which predicts from hand-crafted statistical features): $\tau=0.934 \pm 0.001$ vs $\tau=0.922 \pm 0.001$ ($\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$) and $\tau=0.915 \pm 0.002$ (STATNN) on CIFAR-10-GS; and $\tau=0.931 \pm 0.005$ vs $0.856 \pm 0.001$ and $0.843$ on SVHN-GS, respectively (uncertainties are min/max over two runs).

metadata.narrative: The reported performance advantage on the Small CNN Zoo rests on only two runs per method (P2), providing insufficient statistical evidence to confidently rank NFN_HNP above NFN_NP or STATNN. The differences are small on CIFAR-10-GS and larger on SVHN-GS, but without more runs the reliability of the quantitative ranking is uncertain. No highlight was identified because the experimental design does not incorporate an element that meaningfully elevates the conclusion's credibility beyond typical empirical practice.

nodes.title: NFN_HNP achieves state-of-the-art correlation with test accuracy on CNN generalization prediction

nodes.content: Equivariant invariant neural functionals built from NF-Layers achieve substantially higher train and test classification accuracies than Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) baselines (with or without permutation augmentation, where training data is augmented with random neuron permutations) on datasets of Implicit Neural Representations (INRs), each encoded by a SIREN (a network with sinusoidal activations). For CIFAR-10 INRs, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ test accuracy is $46.6\%\pm0.072$ vs MLP $16.9\%\pm0.250$; for MNIST INRs, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ test accuracy is $92.9\%\pm0.218$ vs MLP $14.5\%\pm0.035$; for 3D ShapeNet-10 INRs, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ test accuracy is $88.7\%\pm0.461$ vs MLP $25.4\%\pm0.121$ and inr2vec $39.1\%\pm0.385$ (uncertainties are standard error over three runs). These results hold when processing SIREN INRs trained from independent random initializations.

metadata.narrative: Strong quantitative evidence (H3) across five datasets with standard errors shows large and consistent improvements over baselines. The differences are substantial and well-characterized statistically, supporting the conclusion that equivariant NFNs outperform non-equivariant methods on INR classification.

nodes.title: Equivariant NFNs outperform non-equivariant MLP baselines on classifying INR weights

nodes.content: A conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) whose encoder and decoder are implemented with equivariant NF-Layers (NFN architecture) can predict 95% sparsity masks (termed "winning tickets" from the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis) from initializations such that training with the predicted masks recovers test accuracies close to those of masks found by iterative magnitude pruning (IMP). On CIFAR-10 CNNs (three convolutional layers with 128 channels plus two fully connected layers), IMP test accuracy is $44.0\%\pm0.06$, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ predicted-ticket accuracy is $41.4\%\pm0.08$; on MNIST MLPs (three-layer MLP with 128 hidden units), IMP test accuracy is $96.2\%\pm0.04$, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ predicted-ticket accuracy is $94.8\%\pm0.01$ (random masks achieve $21.1\%$ on CIFAR-10 and $89.6\%$ on MNIST; uncertainties are standard error over initializations).

metadata.narrative: The winning-ticket prediction results (H4) demonstrate that NFNs can predict effective masks from initialization on the tested architectures, coming close to IMP performance. However, P3 highlights that the experiments are limited to small networks (MLP on MNIST, small CNN on CIFAR-10) with only 400 training pairs, so the generality of the claim is not established. The conclusion holds for the tested regimes but requires further validation for larger or more diverse architectures.

nodes.title: Neural functionals predict winning-ticket masks from initialization near IMP performance

nodes.content: Composing equivariant NF-Layers into an NFN that outputs additive edits $U' = U + \gamma \cdot \mathrm{NFN}(U)$ to INR weights (where $\gamma$ is a learned scalar initialized to $0.01$) yields edited INRs whose generated images have lower mean squared error (MSE) to ground-truth image-space transformations (e.g., dilating MNIST digits or increasing contrast on CIFAR-10) than edits produced by MLP baselines. Numerical results: MSE on Dilate (MNIST) is $0.068$ for $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ vs $0.306$ for MLP; MSE on Contrast (CIFAR-10) is $0.020$ for $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ vs $0.031$ for MLP (lower is better). Qualitative inspection confirms that NFNs produce edited images visually closer to the target transformation than MLP baselines.

metadata.narrative: The quantitative editing results lack error bars (P4), undermining the reliability of the reported MSE improvements. However, the qualitative comparisons (H5) provide visual evidence that NFNs produce more faithful edits. The conclusion that NFNs enable effective weight-space editing is partially supported by the qualitative results, but the quantitative claims remain uncertain.

nodes.title: Equivariant NFNs enable weight-space style editing of INRs with lower MSE than MLP baselines

nodes.content: Empirically, the pointwise ablation NF-Layer that uses only the local term $d^i W_{jk}^{(i)}$ (denoted $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{PT}}$) performs comparably to full equivariant NFNs on the winning-ticket mask prediction task: $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{PT}}$ test accuracy is $42.6\%\pm0.07$ on CIFAR-10 CNNs and $95.0\%\pm0.01$ on MNIST MLPs, close to $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ ($41.4\%\pm0.08$ and $94.8\%\pm0.01$ respectively). This suggests that simple per-weight scoring can suffice for predicting masks in these settings. In contrast, on weight-space editing tasks (Dilate on MNIST and Contrast on CIFAR-10), $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{PT}}$ performs significantly worse: test MSE on Dilate is $0.197$ vs $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ $0.068$, and on Contrast is $0.029$ vs $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ $0.020$. This indicates that modeling interactions between weights and layers is important for transformations requiring coordinated spatial or geometric changes.

metadata.narrative: H6 shows that NFN_PT performs comparably to full NFNs on winning-ticket prediction, supporting the claim that pointwise processing suffices for that task. The claim that NFN_PT fails on editing tasks relies on the same editing experiment lacking error bars (P5), so the editing failure is not robustly established. The conclusion is partially supported: the success part is well-evidenced, while the failure part is uncertain.

nodes.title: Pointwise NF-Layer ablation (NFN_PT) suffices for winning-ticket prediction but is insufficient for editing

nodes.content: The NP-equivariant NF-Layer is described via pseudocode, and code for models and all experiments is released at https://github.com/AllanYangZhou/nfn.

metadata.narrative: The code release and pseudocode (H7) provide a practical implementation, enabling reproducibility and further use. No uncertainties affect this conclusion.

nodes.title: Implementation details and code release for NP-equivariant NF-Layer

nodes.content: For an L-layer feedforward network with hidden-layer permutation group $\tilde{\mathcal{S}} = \prod_{i=1}^{L-1} S_{n_i}$, the derivation of the $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$-equivariant linear NF-Layer partitions the parameter tensor $\theta$ into orbits under $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$ and yields parameter-sharing constraints that distinguish layer pairs $(i,s)$ and whether layers are input ($i=1$), output ($i=L$), or hidden ($1<i<L$). The analysis for sub-blocks involving boundary layers (e.g., $i=1,s=1$; $i=1,s=L$; $i=L,s=1$; $i=L,s=L$) introduces additional parameters that depend on the input dimension $n_0$ and output dimension $n_L$. However, the derivation does not provide a step-by-step verification that all orbits within these boundary sub-blocks are correctly enumerated, nor does it explicitly prove that the resulting constraints cover all possible $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$-equivariant linear maps.

metadata.failure_mode: If the parameter sharing is incomplete (missing some orbits), then the HNP layer H̃ may fail to represent certain linear HNP-equivariant maps, contradicting the claim that H̃ is the "full" HNP-equivariant layer. Consequently, the theoretical foundation for experiments using NFN_HNP (e.g., generalization prediction) would be weakened: the architecture would be one specific equivariant layer rather than a complete characterization. However, the practical impact on experimental performance might be limited if the missing maps are not beneficial for the tasks.
metadata.weakness_reason: The orbit analysis for HNP is presented as tables without a formal proof of completeness akin to Proposition 1 for NP. The derivation in Appendix C.1 summarizes the orbit counting but does not verify each sub-block exhaustively. The complexity of boundaries (input/output layers) introduces many special cases; without explicit verification for each, it is plausible that some orbits are merged or missed, leading to either over-constrained (not expressive enough) or under-constrained (overly permissive) parameter sharing.

nodes.title: Potential incompleteness in HNP parameter-sharing derivation

nodes.content: In the CNN generalization prediction experiment on the Small CNN Zoo subsets CIFAR-10-GS and SVHN-GS, the performance of each method ($\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$, and STATNN) is evaluated using only two runs. The Kendall's $\tau$ values and their reported uncertainties ($\pm$ min/max over two runs) provide a small sample for comparison. For example, the difference between $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$ and $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ on CIFAR-10-GS is $0.012$ ($0.934$ vs $0.922$) with ranges $\pm 0.001$, but with only two runs, the stability of these numbers is unknown and no significance test is provided.

metadata.failure_mode: If the observed performance advantage of NFN_HNP is not statistically reliable, the conclusion that NFN_HNP "achieves higher rank-correlation" than NFN_NP and STATNN may be premature. The conclusion's quantitative ranking could flip with more runs, and the claim of best performance on these benchmarks would be unsupported.
metadata.weakness_reason: Two runs are insufficient to assess sampling variability. The uncertainty reported as min/max over two runs gives the range but not a reliable confidence interval. The small differences could be overturned with additional runs. Standard practice in benchmark comparisons often uses 3-5 runs with standard error; here only two runs are used, which is weaker.

nodes.title: Insufficient statistical evidence from two runs in generalization prediction experiment

nodes.content: The winning-ticket prediction experiments use datasets of (initialization, mask) pairs with only 400 training examples and 50 test examples, derived from a three-layer MLP with 128 hidden units trained on MNIST and a small CNN with three convolutional layers (128 channels) and two fully connected layers trained on CIFAR-10. The scale of networks and the number of training pairs are modest. Generalization of the claim to larger networks (e.g., ResNets, Transformers) or to other sparsity levels beyond 95% is not tested.

metadata.failure_mode: If the claim is interpreted broadly as "neural functionals can predict winning tickets from initialization" without qualification, the limited experimental scope would not justify that general claim. The conclusion as stated in the paper might be interpreted as a general capability, but the experiments only support it for the specific settings tested. A reader expecting the method to work on, e.g., ImageNet-scale classifiers would be unsupported. The conclusion would become weaker or invalid outside its test regime.
metadata.weakness_reason: The dataset size (400 pairs) is relatively small; the networks are small. The task is specific to 95% sparsity and a single pruning strategy (one-step IMP). It is not shown that the learned mapping transfers to networks with more layers, wider layers, different activation functions, or different pruning criteria. Without evidence on larger or more diverse architectures, the conclusion's scope is limited.

nodes.title: Limited scale and scope of winning-ticket prediction experiments

nodes.content: In the weight-space style editing experiments (Dilate on MNIST, Contrast on CIFAR-10), the test mean squared error (MSE) for each method ($\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{PT}}$, MLP, and $\mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{Aug}}$) is reported as a single value without error bars or multiple runs. For example, on the Dilate task, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ MSE is $0.068$ vs MLP $0.306$, while on the Contrast task, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ MSE is $0.020$ vs MLP $0.031$. Without uncertainty quantification, the stability and statistical significance of these results are unknown.

metadata.failure_mode: If the experimental results are not reproducible or the observed improvement is within random variation, the conclusion that NFNs enable better editing (lower MSE) would be unsupported. The quantitative advantage claimed in the conclusion could be an artifact of a single run.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper provides no indication of the number of runs or any variance measure. For a single run, the result could be affected by random seeds, training variability, or data splits. Standard practice for machine learning experiments is to report error bars over multiple runs (at least 3). The absence of such reporting reduces confidence in the quantitative improvement.

nodes.title: Editing experiment results lack error bars

nodes.content: The claim that the pointwise ablation $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{PT}}$ fails on editing tasks is based on the same editing experiment (Dilate on MNIST and Contrast on CIFAR-10) that lacks error bars or multiple runs. While $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{PT}}$'s test MSE on the Dilate task ($0.197$) is larger than $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$'s ($0.068$), the magnitude of the gap and its reliability are uncertain without replicate runs.

metadata.failure_mode: If the results are not robust, the conclusion that cross-weight interactions are necessary for editing would be weakened. The relative failure of NFN_PT could be due to run variability rather than architectural limitation.
metadata.weakness_reason: Same as P4: no uncertainty quantification. The conclusion that NFN_PT "fails on editing tasks" may be overstated if the results are not stable.

nodes.title: Editing failure claim for NFN_PT lacks error bars

nodes.content: The NP-equivariant NF-Layer H (Eq. 2) is derived through a complete orbit analysis of the linear map parameter tensor under the full neuron permutation group S = ∏_{i=0}^L S_{n_i}, resulting in an explicit formula with O(L^2) free parameter blocks (in the multi-channel case, each block is a c_o × c_i matrix). Proposition 1 states that H is S-equivariant and any linear S-equivariant map can be represented in this form; the proof is provided in Appendix B through parameter-sharing constraints (Table 7) and simplification to Eq. 2.

metadata.credit: The formal derivation and completeness proof establish that the NP NF-Layer is a universal linear S-equivariant map on weight space, providing a principled foundation for building equivariant neural functionals. Without this characterization, one could not guarantee that a composition of such layers could express all equivariant functions, and the framework would lack theoretical grounding. The explicit formula and parameter count further guide practical implementation and scaling analysis.

nodes.title: Formal proof and explicit NP NF-Layer formula

nodes.content: For the HNP setting (hidden-layer permutation symmetry), the equivariant linear NF-Layer H̃ is specified by the parameter-sharing constraints in Tables 8-11, which partition the parameter tensor θ into orbits under the HNP group S̃ = ∏_{i=1}^{L-1} S_{n_i}. The tables cover all sub-blocks of the index space, including boundary layers (i=1, s=1; i=1, s=L; i=L, s=1; i=L, s=L) with explicit handling of input and output dimensions.

metadata.credit: The tables provide a concrete, implementable specification for the HNP-equivariant layer, enabling construction of NFN_HNP used in experiments. Without this detailed parameter sharing, practitioners would have to re-derive the layer from first principles, and the scalability analysis (parameter count O(ci co (L + n0 + n_L)^2)) would be unavailable. The tables also serve as a reference for future work on weight-space architectures with boundary conditions.

nodes.title: Explicit HNP parameter-sharing tables

nodes.content: On three image INR datasets (CIFAR-10, MNIST, FashionMNIST) and two 3D shape INR datasets (ShapeNet-10, ScanNet-10), equivariant NFN architectures (NFN_NP and NFN_HNP) achieve test classification accuracies substantially higher than MLP baselines (with and without permutation augmentation) and the inr2vec baseline: e.g., NFN_NP attains 46.6% on CIFAR-10 versus MLP 16.9%, 92.9% on MNIST versus MLP 14.5%, and 88.7% on ShapeNet-10 versus inr2vec 39.1%. Uncertainties are standard errors over three runs, and the improvements are consistent across all datasets.

metadata.credit: The large and consistent accuracy gaps across diverse INR types (2D images, 3D shapes) and the use of standard error over three runs provide strong quantitative evidence that incorporating permutation symmetry via NF-Layers substantially benefits weight-space classification. The results rule out the possibility that the poor performance of MLP baselines is attributable to capacity or tuning, as larger MLPs also underperform (Table 15). This directly supports the conclusion that equivariant NFNs outperform non-equivariant methods on INR classification.

nodes.title: Strong and consistent empirical improvement across INR classification datasets

nodes.content: In the winning-ticket mask prediction task, the NFN_NP-based conditional VAE produces masks that, when used to train from initialization, achieve test accuracies close to those of masks found by iterative magnitude pruning (IMP): 41.4% (NFN_NP) vs 44.0% (IMP) on CIFAR-10, and 94.8% vs 96.2% on MNIST. Performance significantly exceeds random masks (21.1% and 89.6%). Uncertainties are standard errors over initializations.

metadata.credit: The results show that an equivariant generative model can learn to predict effective sparsity masks from initialization alone, nearly matching the computationally expensive IMP procedure. This demonstrates a new capability for weight-space processing and supports the conclusion that neural functionals can predict winning tickets. The gap to IMP is small enough to be practically meaningful.

nodes.title: Winning-ticket prediction close to IMP performance

nodes.content: In the INR style editing task, qualitative comparisons (Figure 4) show that edited images from NFN_NP and NFN_HNP more closely match the ground-truth transformed images (dilated MNIST digits, enhanced contrast CIFAR-10) than those from MLP baselines. For example, MLP-edited dilated digits appear less filled, while NFN-edited ones retain thickness comparable to ground truth.

metadata.credit: The qualitative evidence directly illustrates that the equivariant architecture produces coherent weight-space transformations that translate to visually faithful image-space edits, supporting the conclusion that NFNs enable effective weight-space style editing. This complements the quantitative MSE results (though those lack error bars) and provides a concrete demonstration of the method's capability.

nodes.title: Qualitative visual improvement for weight-space editing

nodes.content: On the winning-ticket mask prediction task, the pointwise ablation NFN_PT achieves test accuracies of 42.6% (CIFAR-10) and 95.0% (MNIST), similar to the full NFN_NP (41.4% and 94.8%). Uncertainties are standard errors over initializations. This shows that per-weight processing suffices for predicting masks in these settings.

metadata.credit: The ablation demonstrates that the success on mask prediction does not require modeling cross-weight interactions, distinguishing it from tasks like editing that do. This finding guides architecture selection and provides insight into the nature of the winning-ticket prediction problem.

nodes.title: Pointwise ablation matches full NFN on winning-ticket prediction

nodes.content: The paper provides pseudocode for the NP-equivariant NF-Layer (Appendix A) and releases a complete code repository at https://github.com/AllanYangZhou/nfn, implementing the models and experiments.

metadata.credit: The code release allows independent verification of results and enables researchers to build upon the framework without re-implementation, directly supporting the conclusion that the paper offers a practical implementation for neural functionals.

steps.reasoning: Define the input weight-space and the neuron-permutation group used throughout the construction: let $L$ be the number of layers, and for each layer $i$ let $n_i$ denote the number of neurons at that layer; denote by $W=\{W^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^L$ the collection of weight matrices where each $W^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i\times n_{i-1}}$ and by $v=\{v^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^L$ the biases where each $v^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i}$; denote the combined weight-space object as $U:=(W,v)$ and its space as $\mathcal{U}:=\mathcal{W}\times\mathcal{V}$. This sets the domain of the linear maps to follow.

Specify the action of a neuron-permutation $\sigma=(\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_L)$ on the weight-space indices (this is the group action the equivariance must respect): for any weight index triple $(i,j,k)$ with $i$ the layer, $j$ a row index and $k$ a column index, define
$\;[\sigma W]_{jk}^{(i)} = W_{\sigma_i^{-1}(j),\,\sigma_{i-1}^{-1}(k)}^{(i)}\;$ and for biases define $\;[\sigma v]_j^{(i)} = v_{\sigma_i^{-1}(j)}^{(i)}\,$.
Here $S_{n_i}$ denotes the symmetric group on $n_i$ elements, and the full neuron-permutation group is $\mathcal{S}=\prod_{i=0}^L S_{n_i}$. Reproducing this action makes explicit which indices are permuted and how equivariance is tested.

Allow multi-channel weight-space features: define $c_i$ input channels and $c_o$ output channels and interpret each $W_{jk}^{(i)}$ as a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{c_i}$ when $c_i>1$; accordingly each linear parameter mapping input channels to output channels is a matrix in $\mathbb{R}^{c_o\times c_i}$. This makes explicit how the single-channel formulas extend to the multi-channel case.

Formulate the general linear map on weight-space as a flattened matrix-vector product so that linear NF-Layers correspond to matrices acting on $\operatorname{vec}(U)$: write an arbitrary linear map as $T(\cdot;\theta):\operatorname{vec}(U)\mapsto \theta\,\operatorname{vec}(U)$ where $\operatorname{vec}(U)\in\mathbb{R}^{\dim(\mathcal{U})}$ flattens $U$ and $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{\dim(\mathcal{U})\times\dim(\mathcal{U})}$ is the parameter matrix. This step makes precise the search space (all linear maps) that equivariance constraints will restrict.

Use the equivariance constraint on the flattened linear map to derive parameter-sharing conditions: require that for every permutation $\sigma\in\mathcal{S}$ the map satisfy $P_\sigma\,\theta=\theta\,P_\sigma$, where $P_\sigma$ is the permutation matrix representing $\sigma$ acting on $\operatorname{vec}(U)$. Expanding this indexwise implies the necessary condition $\theta_{\beta}^{\alpha}=\theta_{\sigma(\beta)}^{\sigma(\alpha)}$ for all index pairs $[\alpha,\beta]$, so the entries of $\theta$ must be constant on orbits under the group action on index pairs. This is the general "parameter-sharing by orbit" principle used to derive NF-Layer structure. [51]

Partition the index space of $\theta$ into the four natural blocks that arise from weights and biases: $\mathbb{I}^{W W}=\mathbb{W}\times\mathbb{W}$, $\mathbb{I}^{W V}=\mathbb{W}\times\mathbb{V}$, $\mathbb{I}^{V W}=\mathbb{V}\times\mathbb{W}$, and $\mathbb{I}^{V V}=\mathbb{V}\times\mathbb{V}$, where $\mathbb{W}$ indexes weight entries $(i,j,k)$ and $\mathbb{V}$ indexes bias entries $(i,j)$. Analyze each sub-block independently because the group action preserves layer indices, so each sub-block further decomposes by layer-pair $(i,s)$; within each sub-block one enumerates the orbits determined by equalities among the row/column indices (e.g., $j=p$, $k=q$, $k=p$, etc.). This makes explicit the combinatorial classification used to reduce $\theta$.

Specialize the orbit partitioning in the weight-weight block to obtain a small set of shared parameters per layer pair: for a representative case where the source layer $s=i-1$, partition $\{[(i,j,k),(s,p,q)]\}$ into two orbits characterized by whether $p=k$ or $p\neq k$; the parameter contributions from this sub-block simplify to a term proportional to the global sum $W_{\star,\star}^{(i-1)}$ plus a term proportional to the row-sum $W_{k,\star}^{(i-1)}$ after reparameterization. Concretely, summing the constrained parameters yields the identity
$\sum_{p,q}\vartheta_{i-1,p,q}^{i,j,k}W_{p q}^{(i-1)} = a^{i,i-1}W_{\star,\star}^{(i-1)} + (b^{i,i-1}-a^{i,i-1})W_{k,\star}^{(i-1)}$,
and reparameterizing gives two additive terms of the NF-Layer form. This step is an explicit algebraic reduction from orbit-constant $\theta$ entries to row/column/global-sum features.

Collect analogous simplifications across all sub-blocks and reparameterize to obtain the per-entry NF-Layer formula: for every layer $i$ and indices $j,k$ define the output entry $H(W)_{jk}^{(i)}$ as the sum of six terms, each corresponding to one of the orbit-types that arise from parameter-sharing:
$\displaystyle H(W)_{jk}^{(i)}=\left(\sum_{s} a^{i,s} W_{\star,\star}^{(s)}\right)+b^{i,i} W_{\star, k}^{(i)}+b^{i,i-1} W_{k,\star}^{(i-1)}+c^{i,i} W_{j,\star}^{(i)}+c^{i,i+1} W_{\star,j}^{(i+1)}+d^{i} W_{jk}^{(i)}$.
Here $W_{\star,\star}^{(s)}$ denotes summing (or averaging) over both row and column indices of $W^{(s)}$, $W_{\star,k}^{(i)}$ sums over rows, $W_{j,\star}^{(i)}$ sums over columns, and $W_{jk}^{(i)}$ is the local element; in the multi-channel case each scalar coefficient (e.g., $a^{i,s}$) is a $c_o\times c_i$ matrix. This formula is the NF-Layer presented in the paper and is obtained directly by the orbit partitioning and reparameterization described above. Fig. 2

Verify equivariance of the NF-Layer formula under the neuron-permutation action: substitute the group action $[\sigma W]_{jk}^{(i)} = W_{\sigma_i^{-1}(j),\sigma_{i-1}^{-1}(k)}^{(i)}$ into the NF-Layer formula and observe that each aggregated term (global sums, row-sums, column-sums, and local elements) transforms consistently so that $[\sigma H(W)]_{jk}^{(i)} = H(\sigma W)_{jk}^{(i)}$ for all $\sigma$, $i$, $j$, $k$. This algebraic check confirms that $H$ is $\mathcal{S}$-equivariant by construction.

Establish universality within the class of linear $\mathcal{S}$-equivariant maps by invoking that any linear map satisfying the equivariance constraint must have the same orbit-wise parameter sharing and therefore can be written in the NF-Layer form: because the equivariance constraint forces $\theta$ to be constant on orbits under $\mathcal{S}$ and because Table 7 (the explicit orbit analysis) enumerates exactly the orbit types that lead to the six terms above, every linear $\mathcal{S}$-equivariant map $T:\mathcal{U}^{c_i}\to\mathcal{U}^{c_o}$ is representable by choosing appropriate parameters $a^{i,s},b^{i,\cdot},c^{i,\cdot},d^i$. This is the statement of the proposition asserting both equivariance and completeness (universality among linear equivariant maps). [51] Table 7

State the alternate symmetry assumption (hidden neuron permutation, HNP): define the HNP group $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}=\prod_{i=1}^{L-1} S_{n_i}$ which permutes only the hidden-layer neuron indices (layers $1,\ldots,L-1$) while leaving input-layer columns and output-layer rows unpermuted. This makes explicit which indices the weaker symmetry preserves and which it does not.

Begin with the same flattened linear-map viewpoint as in the NP case: represent a linear map $T(\cdot;\theta):\operatorname{vec}(U)\mapsto\theta\,\operatorname{vec}(U)$ and enforce equivariance to $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$ by requiring $P_\sigma\,\theta=\theta\,P_\sigma$ for all $\sigma\in\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$. This implies, as before, that entries of $\theta$ must be constant on orbits of the $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$ action on index-pairs. The derivation strategy therefore parallels the NP case but with a different group action.

Analyze how the restricted action of $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$ changes orbit structure compared to the NP setting: because input-layer column indices (columns of $W^{(1)}$) are never permuted and output-layer row indices (rows of $W^{(L)}$ and entries of $v^{(L)}$) are never permuted, sub-blocks of the parameter index space that involve these input/output indices decompose into many more distinct orbits (one per fixed input/output index) than in the NP case where those indices are permuted. This observation explains why the HNP parameter-sharing yields additional parameters that scale with $n_0$ and $n_L$.

Carry out the orbit partitioning within each sub-block $\mathbb{I}^{WW},\mathbb{I}^{WV},\mathbb{I}^{VW},\mathbb{I}^{VV}$ as in the NP derivation but using the $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$ action, treating special cases when $i$ or $s$ equals $1$ (input layer) or $L$ (output layer): for example, in the sub-block $\mathbb{I}_{1,1}^{WW}$ (where $i=s=1$) the column indices $k,q$ are fixed and not permuted, so there are two orbits for every pair of fixed columns $(k,q)$ characterized by whether $j=p$; hence this sub-block contributes $2n_0^2$ distinct orbit-parameters instead of a constant number. Tables enumerating these orbit-dependent parameters are produced by this analysis.

Present the concrete parameter-sharing pattern resulting from the $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$ orbit partitioning: collect the orbit-constant parameters into tabulated forms that specify which indices are tied and which remain distinct, handling the multiple cases that arise depending on whether layer indices are input/output/hidden and whether layers are adjacent or equal. These parameter-sharing tables are given explicitly (in the paper) as Tables 8–11, one table per parameter tensor ($\vartheta,\phi,\varphi,\psi$), and they fully specify how to tie entries of the flattened parameter $\theta$ to obtain the HNP-equivariant linear NF-Layer $\tilde{H}$.

Count how the resulting free parameter blocks scale: because some sub-blocks now introduce parameters proportional to $n_0$ or $n_L$ (or their squares, when both input and output indices are fixed), the total number of free parameter blocks after HNP equivariant sharing grows as $O\!\big(c_i c_o (L + n_0 + n_L)^2\big)$ when accounting for multi-channel input/output; this is the scaling reported in the paper for $\tilde{H}$ after applying the HNP parameter-sharing pattern.

Note the practical consequence emphasized by the authors: the HNP-equivariant layer $\tilde{H}$ is the full linear characterization for equivariance to hidden-layer permutations but can be parameter-inefficient and computationally prohibitive in settings with large input or output dimensionalities due to the additional dependence on $n_0$ and $n_L$. This motivates considering the NP layer or IO-encoding in practice when input/output dimensions are large.

Define an $\mathcal{S}$-invariant pooling map that reduces weight-space features to a fixed-dimensional vector by summing (or averaging) across indices that the symmetry permutes: for full neuron-permutation symmetry $\mathcal{S}$, define $P:\mathcal{U}\to\mathbb{R}^{2L}$ by
$\;P(U)=(W_{\star,\star}^{(1)},\ldots,W_{\star,\star}^{(L)},\,v_{\star}^{(1)},\ldots,v_{\star}^{(L)})\,$,
where $W_{\star,\star}^{(i)}$ denotes summing (or averaging) over both rows and columns of $W^{(i)}$ and $v_{\star}^{(i)}$ denotes summing over entries of $v^{(i)}$. This constructs a permutation-invariant summary by reducing each permutable axis.

Define the HNP-appropriate invariant pooling that only sums over axes that are permuted by the hidden-neuron group $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$: because input-layer columns and output-layer rows are not permuted under $\tilde{\mathcal{S}}$, the HNP-invariant map $\tilde{P}:\mathcal{U}\to\mathbb{R}^{2L+n_0+2n_L}$ augments the NP-summary with per-input/ per-output partial sums as necessary; concretely the paper defines
$\displaystyle \tilde{P}(U)=\big(P(U),\,W_{\star,:}^{(1)},\,W_{:,\star}^{(L)},\,v^{(L)}\big)$,
where $W_{\star,:}^{(1)}$ sums only rows of $W^{(1)}$, $W_{:,\star}^{(L)}$ sums only columns of $W^{(L)}$, and $v^{(L)}$ is included unchanged. This is an explicit formula that captures which sums are valid under HNP invariance. Table 1

Explain composition to produce invariant neural functionals: since the composition of an equivariant map followed by an invariant map is invariant, stacking equivariant NF-Layers (which are linear equivariant layers plus pointwise nonlinearities) to produce weight-space features, and then applying $P$ or $\tilde{P}$ produces an invariant neural functional that outputs a permutation-invariant vector summary suitable for downstream MLP heads or scalar predictions. This step states the standard composition property used by the authors to build invariant functionals.

Specify the structural difference in convolutional weight tensors: for a 1D convolutional layer with filter width $w$, define the layer weights as $W^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i\times n_{i-1}\times w}$ where $n_i$ and $n_{i-1}$ are the output and input channel counts and $w$ indexes spatial filter positions; denote the per-filter vector as $W_{jk}^{(i)}:=W_{j,k,:}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^w$, making explicit the tensor indexing that will be treated by the NF-Layer.

Observe that the spatial filter dimension is not permuted by neuron permutations and so behaves like additional non-permuted channels: fold the filter width into the channel dimension by concatenating the $w$ filter positions with any existing feature channels, so that the multi-channel weight representation becomes $W^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_i\times n_{i-1}\times(cw)}$ when there are $c$ feature channels. This recasts convolutional filters as multi-channel weights compatible with the multi-channel NF-Layer $H:\mathcal{U}^{cw_i}\to\mathcal{U}^{cw_o}$.

State the implementation consequence: by treating spatial filter dimensions as additional channel dimensions and using the multi-channel NF-Layer implementation, the NP-equivariant NF-Layer $H$ (and its multi-channel form) directly apply to convolutional weight spaces; similarly, 2D convolutional spatial dimensions can be combined into channels in the same way. This construction enables processing CNN weight-space inputs using the same NF-Layer machinery as for fully connected weights.

Note subtleties with mixed convolutional and fully-connected stacks: when a convolutional layer is followed by a globally pooled output that becomes input to a fully-connected layer (common in many CNN classifiers), global spatial pooling removes spatial dimensions and the same permutation action on channels and the NF-Layer definitions apply without modification; more complex flattening strategies (nontrivial spatial dimension flattening) are left for future treatment. This documents the boundary conditions for the convolutional extension.

State the practical problem motivating IO-encoding: the NP-equivariant NF-Layer $H$ assumes that input and output neuron indices are permutable, which enforces parameter sharing that makes the layer parameter-efficient but prevents the layer from representing functions that distinguish input or output indices (i.e., IO-asymmetric tasks). This identifies the modeling limitation that IO-encoding aims to address.

Describe the IO-encoding mechanism precisely: add positional embeddings to the columns of the first-layer weight matrices $W^{(1)}$ (i.e., to input-side indices), to the rows of the last-layer weight matrices $W^{(L)}$ (i.e., to output-side indices), and to the final biases $v^{(L)}$; these positional embeddings may be learned parameters or fixed sinusoidal encodings. Adding these position embeddings makes certain columns/rows distinguishable under the NP permutation action, thereby breaking the effective symmetry at inputs and outputs while retaining the NP equivariant parameter-sharing for all other entries.

Give the concrete sinusoidal encoding used in experiments as an explicit example: the experiments use sinusoidal positional encodings with a maximum frequency of $10$ and $6$ frequency bands, producing embedding dimensionality $13$ (i.e., 6 frequencies $\times$ 2 plus a constant term), which are concatenated to the corresponding columns/rows so that the NF-Layer receives these position-dependent features. This specifies a concrete instantiation of IO-encoding used in practice. Table 14

State the empirical effect reported in the paper: applying IO-encoding permits the NP-equivariant layer $H$ to model IO-asymmetric functions while keeping the NP parameter-sharing; empirically, IO-encoding makes $H$ competitive or superior to the (more parameter-rich) HNP layer $\tilde{H}$ in tasks where IO asymmetry matters, while using far fewer parameters. This summarizes the experimental finding that IO-encoding closes much of the expressivity gap caused by NP assumptions.

Recall the unconstrained parameter count for a general linear map on $c_i$-channel inputs to $c_o$-channel outputs: since a general linear map $T:\mathcal{U}^{c_i}\to\mathcal{U}^{c_o}$ flattened to $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{\dim(\mathcal{U})c_o\times\dim(\mathcal{U})c_i}$ has $c_i c_o \dim(\mathcal{U})^2$ scalar parameters, this gives the baseline parameter scaling without any equivariance constraints.

Use the orbit-analysis argument to derive the NP-equivariant parameter count scaling: because the NP parameter-sharing ties entries across each layer-pair and the number of distinct orbit-types per $(i,s)$ pair is constant (independent of $n_i$), the total number of free parameter blocks after NP equivariant sharing grows with the number of layer pairs, i.e., $O(L^2)$; multiplying by the $c_i c_o$ channel matrices yields $O\!\big(c_i c_o L^2\big)$ free parameter blocks for the NP-equivariant layer $H$.

Use the HNP orbit-structure to derive its scaling: because under HNP some sub-blocks generate parameters that depend on input and output dimensions ($n_0$ and $n_L$) — for example, sub-blocks involving $W^{(1)}$ columns or $W^{(L)}$ rows produce $O(n_0)$ or $O(n_L)$ multiplicity of orbits — the total free parameter blocks after HNP equivariant sharing scale as $O\!\big(c_i c_o (L + n_0 + n_L)^2\big)$.

Summarize the comparative tradeoffs: contrast the unconstrained $c_i c_o \dim(\mathcal{U})^2$ parameter count with the two equivariant scalings above to quantify how stronger symmetry assumptions (NP) dramatically reduce parameters to $O(c_i c_o L^2)$ at the cost of assuming IO-permutability, while the weaker HNP assumption yields higher parameter counts $O\!\big(c_i c_o (L + n_0 + n_L)^2\big)$ but can represent IO-asymmetric maps without positional encodings. This ties the orbit-count algebra to practical parameter-efficiency considerations reported in the paper. Table 1

Start from the upstream architectural results: use the HNP-equivariant NF-Layer $\tilde{H}$ (conclusion 2) as the primary building block for the NFN referred to as $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$; treat $\tilde{H}$'s equivariance and parameterization as given and available to implement the model used in the experiments.

Describe the dataset and evaluation metric used for the experiment: the Small CNN Zoo benchmark contains many small CNN weights trained on datasets such as CIFAR-10-GS and SVHN-GS; the evaluation metric is Kendall's $\tau$ (a rank correlation coefficient with range $[-1,1]$) between predicted and actual test accuracies of the CNNs, which measures how well the predictor ranks models by generalization performance. [61]

Specify the predictive model architecture and training protocol used for generalization prediction: the NFN used three equivariant NF-Layers with channel widths (16,16,5), ReLU nonlinearities, followed by an invariant mean-pooling NF-Layer, a projection to a 1,000-dimensional vector, and then a two-hidden-layer MLP head (1,000 units per layer) producing a scalar probability trained with binary cross-entropy; training ran for up to 50 epochs with early stopping based on validation $\tau$ and used Adam at learning rate $0.001$ and batch size $8$. These architectural and training details explain how $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$ was instantiated for the reported experiment. Table 12

Report the empirical results and direct comparisons: on CIFAR-10-GS, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$ achieved Kendall's $\tau = 0.934 \pm 0.001$, while the NP variant $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ achieved $\tau = 0.922 \pm 0.001$ and the prior STATNN baseline achieved $\tau = 0.915 \pm 0.002$ (uncertainties are max/min over two runs); on SVHN-GS, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$ achieved $\tau = 0.931 \pm 0.005$ compared to $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ at $0.856 \pm 0.001$ and STATNN at $0.843\pm0.000$. These numerical results show $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$ outperforming both the NP variant and the STATNN baseline on both subsets. Table 2

Explain the authors' interpretation for why $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$ performs best in this setting: because the Small CNN Zoo subsets used here have relatively small input and output dimensionalities, the HNP layer's larger parameter usage is not prohibitively expensive (the paper notes that $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$ used approximately $1.4\times$ the parameters of $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ for comparable depth and channels) while offering greater modeling flexibility by not assuming IO-permutability; this balance explains the superior empirical rank-correlation performance. This step records the authors' stated rationale linking parameter-budget and task-appropriateness.

Begin from the upstream architectural primitives already established: use both NP-equivariant NF-Layer $H$ (conclusion 1) and the HNP-equivariant variant $\tilde{H}$ (conclusion 2) as available building blocks; also, if IO-encoding (conclusion 5) is employed, treat its positional embeddings as part of the NFN input processing. These upstream modules are the basis for constructing invariant NFNs for INR classification.

Describe the INR classification problem and datasets used: the task is to classify the content encoded by implicit neural representations (INRs) trained as SIRENs; datasets include CIFAR-10 INRs, MNIST INRs, FashionMNIST INRs, and 3D-shape INRs (ShapeNet-10 and ScanNet-10). Each INR maps spatial coordinates to pixel (or signed distance) values and the NFN receives only the INR weights as input. The SIREN architectures used in these experiments were three-layer networks with 32 hidden neurons for the image INRs and one hidden layer with 128 neurons for some 3D-shape INRs; SIRENs were trained per image/shape as described in the experimental protocol. [55]

Specify the NFN architectures and training setup used for INR classification: the invariant NFN used three equivariant NF-Layers (with ReLU) each having 512 channels, followed by an invariant mean-pooling NF-Layer and a three-layer MLP head with 1,000 hidden units and ReLU activations (dropout applied to the MLP head); training used Adam with learning rate $1\times 10^{-4}$, batch size $32$, and $2\times 10^5$ training steps. For IO-encoding experiments, sinusoidal positional encodings (max frequency $10$, $6$ frequency bands, dimension $13$) were appended to input/output axes as described earlier. These implementation details explain how the reported NFN results were obtained. Table 14

Report CIFAR-10, MNIST, and 3D-shape INR classification results comparing equivariant NFNs to MLP baselines: for CIFAR-10 INRs $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ test accuracy is $46.6\%\pm0.072$ while MLP achieves $16.9\%\pm0.250$; for MNIST INRs $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ test accuracy is $92.9\%\pm0.218$ while MLP is $14.5\%\pm0.035$; for ShapeNet-10 3D INRs $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ test accuracy is $88.7\%\pm0.461$ while MLP is $25.4\%\pm0.121$ and the recent non-equivariant method inr2vec attains $39.1\%\pm0.385$. These numerical values demonstrate substantially higher test accuracies for equivariant NFNs across image and 3D INR datasets. Table 3 Table 4

Record additional empirical details and robustness claims: the reported uncertainties are standard errors over multiple runs (three runs for the image INRs, per the paper), the NFNs also achieved higher training accuracies (reported in appendix tables), and the NFN advantage persists even when MLP baselines are enlarged or trained with permutation augmentation. The authors additionally note that $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ can match or outperform $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$ on some datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10 and 3D-shape datasets) while using substantially fewer parameters (e.g., $\sim35\%$ of the parameters on CIFAR-10), supporting the claim that NP variants with IO-encoding can be both efficient and accurate.

Treat the NFN architecture and equivariant NF-Layers as given (conclusion 1): implement both encoder and decoder of a conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) using equivariant NF-Layers so that the generative model maps initializations to winning-ticket sparsity masks conditioned on initialization features.

Define the cVAE and objective precisely: let $U_0\in\mathcal{U}$ be an initialization and $M\in\{0,1\}^{\dim(\mathcal{U})}$ be a binary sparsity mask; let $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{\dim(\mathcal{U})\times C}$ be the latent variable with prior $p(Z)$ chosen as an isotropic Gaussian; define encoder $q_\theta(Z\mid U_0,M)$ and decoder $p_\theta(M\mid U_0,Z)$ implemented with equivariant NF-Layers; train by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO):
$\displaystyle \mathcal{L}_\theta(M,U_0)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim q_\theta(\cdot\mid U_0,M)}\big[\ln p_\theta(M\mid U_0,z)\big]-\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q_\theta(\cdot\mid U_0,M)\,\|\,p(\cdot)\big)$.
This makes explicit the probabilistic training objective used to learn to predict masks.

Describe the datasets and experimental protocol used to evaluate predicted winning tickets: for the MNIST experiments the target models are three-layer MLPs with 128 hidden units, and for CIFAR-10 the target models are CNNs with three convolutional layers (128 channels) and two fully-connected layers; training datasets for the cVAE contain 400 (initialization, ticket) pairs used for training and 50 held out for evaluation; tickets are obtained by running one step of iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) at sparsity $P_m=0.95$ to produce ground-truth winning tickets that the cVAE is trained to model. These dataset details define the empirical setting used to compare IMP and NFN-predicted masks. Table 13

Report the quantitative comparison between IMP masks and NFN-predicted masks when used to prune and retrain: on CIFAR-10 CNNs with 95% sparsity, IMP yields test accuracy $44.0\%\pm0.06$, NFN$_{\mathrm{NP}}$ predicted-ticket training yields $41.4\%\pm0.08$, and random masks yield $21.1\%\pm0.26$; on MNIST MLPs with 95% sparsity, IMP yields $96.2\%\pm0.04$, NFN$_{\mathrm{NP}}$ yields $94.8\%\pm0.01$, and random masks yield $89.6\%\pm0.36$. These results show that NFN-predicted masks approach IMP performance and substantially outperform random masks. Table 5

Note the additional observation that the pointwise ablation NFN$_{\mathrm{PT}}$ (which uses only the local per-weight scoring term $d^{i}W_{jk}^{(i)}$) attains comparable predicted-ticket performance in these experiments (e.g., NFN$_{\mathrm{PT}}$ test accuracy $42.6\%\pm0.07$ on CIFAR-10 and $95.0\%\pm0.01$ on MNIST), suggesting that per-weight scoring suffices to approximate IMP in the studied settings; Appendix analysis further suggests NFN$_{\mathrm{PT}}$ behaves similarly to magnitude pruning. This documents the empirical nuance in which a simpler NFN variant is adequate for the winning-ticket prediction task.

Start from the NFN architecture primitives (conclusions 1 and 2): implement an NFN that maps INR weights to additive weight edits by composing equivariant NF-Layers and then applying a learned scalar multiplier $\gamma$ to the NFN output so that the edited weights are $U' = U + \gamma\cdot\mathrm{NFN}(U)$; this defines the editing model architecture used in the experiments.

Define the training objective used to learn the NFN editor: let $\mathrm{SIREN}(x,y;U)$ denote the INR output at coordinates $(x,y)$ for weights $U$, and let $f_i(x,y)$ be the ground-truth image after applying an image-space transformation (e.g., dilation or increased contrast); train the NFN by minimizing mean squared error between the image produced by the edited INR and the ground-truth transformed image:
$\displaystyle \mathcal{L}(\mathrm{NFN})=\frac{1}{N d^2}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{x,y} \big\|\mathrm{SIREN}(x,y;U_i+\gamma\cdot\mathrm{NFN}(U_i)) - f_i(x,y)\big\|_2^2$,
where $N$ is the number of INRs and $d^2$ the number of pixels per image. This explicitly gives the differentiable objective used to backpropagate through the SIREN.

Describe the editing tasks and datasets: two editing tasks are considered — (1) Dilate on MNIST which thickens digits by applying morphological dilation to the ground-truth image, and (2) Contrast on CIFAR-10 which increases image contrast — and training data are constructed by applying these image-space transforms to produce target images for the corresponding INR weights. The NFN must modify weight-space structure so that the edited INR produces the intended image-space transformation.

Report the quantitative mean-squared-error (MSE) results comparing NFN variants to MLP baselines: for the Dilate (MNIST) task the MLP baseline achieves MSE $0.306$, the pointwise NFN$_{\mathrm{PT}}$ achieves $0.197$, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$ achieves $0.070$, and $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ achieves $0.068$; for the Contrast (CIFAR-10) task MLP achieves $0.031$, NFN$_{\mathrm{PT}}$ $0.029$, $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{HNP}}$ $0.021$, and $\mathrm{NFN}_{\mathrm{NP}}$ $0.020$. These numbers demonstrate that equivariant NFNs produce edited INRs whose generated images are quantitatively closer (lower MSE) to the ground-truth transformed images than edits produced by non-equivariant MLP baselines. Table 6

Note qualitative corroboration: the paper supplies qualitative examples of edited INR outputs which show that NFN edits better preserve geometric transformations (e.g., dilations of MNIST digits) and produce images with contrast closer to the ground truth compared to MLP baselines; these qualitative observations support the numerical MSE improvements reported. Begin from previously established empirical findings: conclusions about winning-ticket prediction (conclusion 9) and weight-space editing (conclusion 10) are treated as known experimental results that provide the evidence base for the ablation conclusions to follow.

Define the pointwise NF-Layer ablation used in these experiments: the pointwise NF-Layer uses only the local per-weight term from the general NF-Layer formula, i.e., sets $H(W)_{jk}^{(i)} := d^{i}\,W_{jk}^{(i)}$ (no global, row, or column-sum terms). NFNs using this per-weight scoring layer are denoted NFN$_{\mathrm{PT}}$. This makes explicit what is meant by the "pointwise" ablation.

Report NFN$_{\mathrm{PT}}$ performance on winning-ticket mask prediction and compare to full NFNs: in the winning-ticket experiments (95% sparsity), NFN$_{\mathrm{PT}}$ achieved test accuracies comparable to full equivariant NFNs (e.g., NFN$_{\mathrm{PT}}$ test accuracy $42.6\%\pm0.07$ on CIFAR-10 and $95.0\%\pm0.01$ on MNIST, close to NFN$_{\mathrm{NP}}$ results), showing that simple per-weight scoring is sufficient to predict effective pruning masks in these experimental settings. These numbers are reported in the winning-ticket comparison table. Table 5

Report NFN$_{\mathrm{PT}}$ performance on weight-space editing and contrast with full NFNs: in editing tasks (Dilate and Contrast), NFN$_{\mathrm{PT}}$ performs significantly worse than full equivariant NFNs (e.g., NFN$_{\mathrm{PT}}$ MSE on Dilate $0.197$ vs NFN$_{\mathrm{NP}}$ $0.068$), indicating that the pointwise model fails to capture the interactions between weights and layers necessary for coordinated geometric transformations; these editing results are summarized in the editing MSE table. Table 6

Summarize the authors' conclusion from these ablations: the empirical pattern — NFN$_{\mathrm{PT}}$ sufficing for winning-ticket mask prediction but failing on editing tasks — leads to the interpretation that per-weight scoring can explain much of the structure relevant to pruning in the studied settings (consistent with magnitude-like heuristics discussed in appendix analysis), while performing coordinated, spatially-structured transformations (editing) requires modeling interactions across weights and layers, which the full equivariant NF-Layers provide.

State that a concrete multi-channel pseudocode implementation of the NP-equivariant NF-Layer is provided: the paper presents a PyTorch-like pseudocode class implementing the multi-channel NP NF-Layer with initialization of per-layer parameter tensors and a forward method that computes the six orbit-derived terms and combines them; the class in the pseudocode is named NPLayer, initializes parameters named $\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B},\mathrm{B\_prev},\mathrm{C},\mathrm{C\_next},\mathrm{D}$ with shapes corresponding to layer pairs and channel mappings, and computes the NF-Layer output by forming appropriate sums over rows/columns and applying the parameter tensors. This documents the concrete implementation guidance the authors provide.

Note implementation caveats the authors mention relative to the pseudocode: the actual released implementation extends the pseudocode to support the full weight-space $\mathcal{U}$ (including biases), supports convolutional weight shapes as described in the convolutional extension, and initializes parameters scaled by the NF-Layer fan-in rather than drawing from a standard normal; these practical details are explicitly stated alongside the pseudocode so practitioners can reproduce the implementation faithfully.

Provide the public code repository location for reproduction: the authors release code for models and experiments at the project repository URL https://github.com/AllanYangZhou/nfn, making the implementation and experimental scripts available to readers. This is the explicit practical artifact the paper makes available. [Project repository]

open_questions.content: The authors explicitly acknowledge several unresolved scientific and engineering directions: (1) scaling NF-Layers and NFNs to process the weights of very large networks by reducing activation sizes produced by NF-Layers and improving parameter or compute efficiency; (2) extending the NF-Layer framework to handle weight inputs of more complex architectures beyond basic feedforward and convolutional blocks — specifically ResNet-style architectures and Transformer blocks — including how to treat skip connections, normalization layers, attention parameter tensors, and flattened spatial layouts; (3) more generally, determining practical strategies for defining the appropriate permutation action and equivariant parameter-sharing for architectures with mixed or nonstandard wiring (e.g., when spatial dimensions are flattened into fully connected layers) remains open; and (4) empirical questions remain about when IO-encoding (positional embeddings) suffices to break input/output symmetry versus when the fuller HNP parameter sharing is necessary, particularly in tasks with very large $n_0$ or $n_L$. These limitations and future-work items are explicitly noted in the Conclusion and scattered throughout the text.
